source.title: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendix; no evident garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares batch-normalized and unnormalized networks and reports training and accuracy outcomes, bearing conceptually on V6's claim about normalization and training speed.
record.gate_note: Reports MNIST test accuracy over training steps and ImageNet validation accuracy and steps to a target accuracy. It does not report training classification error, and the ImageNet results combine batch normalization with other recipe changes; these results do not establish the specific training-error claims in V1–V5.
record.test_reason: This is an original source for V6. Its MNIST and Inception comparisons directly measure accuracy versus training steps, and its ImageNet experiments compare successful higher-learning-rate BN recipes with an unnormalized model that diverges.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that BN accelerates training, permits higher learning rates and saturating nonlinearities, and can reduce the need for Dropout. Adding BN alone speeds Inception training; further recipe changes produce the largest speedups and accuracy improvements. Their internal-covariate-shift explanation is a proposed mechanism rather than an independently established causal result.
record.recipe_differences: Tests adding batch normalization to networks and compares training outcomes. Some ImageNet speedup results also change learning rate, Dropout, L2 regularization, learning-rate decay, local response normalization, data shuffling and photometric distortion.
record.method_sensitivity: ImageNet outcomes differ across BN variants and learning rates; BN-x30 starts more slowly but reaches higher final accuracy. MNIST test accuracy is reported over training steps.
record.problems: The ImageNet results that show the largest speedups combine Batch Normalization with several other recipe changes. MNIST accuracy is described without exact numerical values in the text. The paper reports validation accuracy and steps to a target, not training classification error.
record.rows_left_out: No required results omitted. Figure 2 accuracy curves lack exact values in text and are not separately extracted; Figure 4 reports ensemble classification error, which does not measure training speed or the claim's training-error outcome.

untested.parts: CIFAR training classification error, interpolation, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth degradation, identity shortcuts, and the specified initialization alternatives.
Comparative initialization effects on speed and trainable depth.
Initial stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, curvature changes, and edge-of-stability training.
VGG on CIFAR-10 and Fixup residual networks. The higher-learning-rate ImageNet comparisons do not isolate BN from other recipe changes.

missing.what: Original unnormalized Inception diverges when its initial learning rate is increased fivefold to 0.0075, whereas BN-x5 trains successfully at that rate. This explicit control is needed for V6's higher-learning-rate component and is absent from the rows.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are issued because this study is an original source for V6. The record incorrectly lists the normalization-only Inception comparison as untested: BN-Baseline provides that comparison directly.

versions.untested_parts: No CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 training classification error results, and no random or corrupted labels.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student local-minima experiment.
No initialization comparison of the kinds specified.
No learning-rate stability-limit or edge-of-stability experiment.

Does not test the stated VGG/CIFAR-10 or Inception/ImageNet normalization-only comparisons in the version; the reported ImageNet speedup comparison includes further recipe changes. It does not test Fixup.

rows.subject: MNIST network with Batch Normalization
rows.size_stated: 3 fully-connected hidden layers with 100 activations each; 10 output activations
rows.operation_detail: Added batch normalization to each hidden layer; trained with sigmoid activations.
rows.measure: Held-out test accuracy over training steps
rows.value: The batch-normalized network enjoys the higher test accuracy.
rows.note: The text states the BN network has higher test accuracy as training progresses; it does not give exact accuracy values in text.
rows.check: Figure 1(a)'s caption explicitly reports faster training as well as higher test accuracy; the extracted value omits the speed result.

rows.subject: Inception
rows.measure: Training steps to reach 72.2% validation accuracy
rows.note: Reference model used for the reported steps-to-target comparison.
rows.check: Valid reference measurement for R3–R5, but the unnormalized baseline alone cannot establish the comparative effect.

rows.subject: BN-Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Added Batch Normalization before each nonlinearity; otherwise same as Inception.

conditions.value: same as Inception; exact value not stated

rows.measure: Training steps to reach 72.2% validation accuracy
rows.note: Paper says BN-Baseline matches Inception in less than half the number of training steps.
rows.check: Change partial to observed: adding BN alone reduces steps to 72.2% from 31.0 million to 13.3 million. The claim specifies no larger required speedup. Its initial learning rate is 0.0015, since it otherwise matches Inception.

source_check.correct: BN-Baseline inherits Inception's initial learning rate of 0.0015; its steps to 72.2% validation accuracy are 13.3 million versus 31.0 million.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2.2, Figure 3 and network definitions, lines 758–783.
source_check.problem: The exact learning rate is supplied by the stated Inception recipe and BN-Baseline's otherwise identical configuration.

rows.subject: BN-x5
rows.size_stated: Same Inception architecture; 13.6 · 10^6 parameters stated for Inception
rows.operation_detail: Batch Normalization plus increased learning rate and other modifications described in Section 4.2.1.
rows.measure: Training steps to reach 72.2% validation accuracy
rows.note: Paper states BN-x5 needs 14 times fewer steps than Inception to reach 72.2%; this recipe changes more than normalization.
rows.check: The speedup is observed, but belongs to the combined BN recipe. Other changes in Section 4.2.1 prevent attributing its full magnitude solely to BN.

rows.subject: BN-x30
rows.size_stated: Same Inception architecture; 13.6 · 10^6 parameters stated for Inception
rows.operation_detail: Like BN-x5, with Batch Normalization and the Section 4.2.1 modifications; initial learning rate increased 30-fold.
rows.measure: Training steps to reach 72.2% validation accuracy
rows.note: The paper says BN-x30 trains somewhat slower initially but reaches higher final accuracy.
rows.check: The speedup is observed for the combined recipe. Its slower initial training is relative to BN-x5, not evidence that it is slower than unnormalized Inception.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2.2, Figure 3, lines 758–775; recipe, lines 791–792; interpretation, lines 814–818.

rows.subject: BN-x5-Sigmoid
rows.size_stated: Same Inception architecture; 13.6 · 10^6 parameters stated for Inception
rows.operation_detail: Like BN-x5 but with sigmoid nonlinearity instead of ReLU.
rows.baseline: Without Batch Normalization, Inception with sigmoid never achieves better than 1/1000 accuracy.
rows.note: This is a BN recipe with additional modifications; the paper's explicit baseline statement concerns original Inception with sigmoid.
rows.check: The text establishes learning to 69.8% while unnormalized sigmoid Inception remains at chance throughout training. This bears on comparative learning progress, although maximum accuracy alone does not quantify speed and the BN recipe includes other changes. Its lower accuracy than ReLU models does not justify partial relative to the sigmoid baseline.

statements.correction: Original study: faster held-out accuracy gains for sigmoid MNIST networks; Inception/ImageNet steps to 72.2% validation accuracy: 31.0 million without BN, 13.3 million with BN alone. VGG/CIFAR-10 attribution requires a different study.
